newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to review Italian budget within a few days.
newsitem.headline: EU to review Italian budget within a few days.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to begin a review of the Italian government's 1997 budget plan within a few days to examine the merits of the so-called "euro tax", officials said on Thursday.
"We are still waiting for the budget," said one Commission official. "It should be arriving in a few days."
The controversial euro tax is a key part of Italy's 1997 budget, tailored to lop 62.5 trillion lire off the 1997 public deficit and speed Italy on its way to EMU membership by 1999.

It may also be an important aspect of Italy's bid to re-join Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), although most think the questionable tax, which some think bears closer resemblance to a loan, could have greater implications for Italy's chances of joining a common currency in 1999.

"In terms of re-joining the ERM I don't think it's a problem, but in terms of being a founding member of EMU, it is a problem," says Bronwyn Curtis, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

To the extent that the tax -- which is expected to be reimbursed to the public after Italy qualifies for monetary union -- raises questions about the durability of Rome's budgetary consolidation, it might prompt countries such as Germany to argue against early EMU membership, analysts said.
"I wouldn't jump into making a link with the ERM. It's tempting but I don't think it will be a deciding factor," said one senior EU monetary official.
Speculation on the lira's ERM re-entry has grown to fever pitch recently, spurred on by the government's strong desire to enter the currency grid by year-end.

Their motivation is largely linked to meeting the currency stability criterion of the Maastricht treaty, which requires membership in the ERM, and the potential budgetary cost savings likely from participation.
It is widely assumed that Italy's debt servicing costs would fall substantially once inside the ERM.

Monetary sources said it seemed certain that if Italy wanted to accomplish its objective this year, it would have to come ahead of the Christmas holiday and the EU summit in Dublin on December 13 and 14.
Such a timetable leaves only a few weekends for the EU's monetary committee, the group responsible for considering ERM applications, to meet.
"It excludes Christmas and you don't want to have it considered around the time of the (EU) summit," said another official.

Regarding Italy's euro tax, Commission officials said they were initially unaware that the proposed tax would in effect be returned to taxpayers after a specified period, an arrangement which under normal circumstances would be classified as a loan.
They added that depending on the outcome of the review, Eurostat, the EU's statistical office, might be asked to offer its own evaluation.

Should such a review determine that the tax could not be applied towards Italy's 1997 budget, the outlook for Italy's deficit would by implication be higher than the 3.3 percent of total output forecast by the Commission in October.
